name: C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency (hereditary angio-oedema)
aliases: hereditary angio-oedema types I and II

clinicalPearls: C1 esterase inhibitor is a serine protease inhibitor (serpin) that restrains the contact (kallikrein-kinin), complement and coagulation systems; its deficiency causes bradykinin-mediated angio-oedema

Hereditary angio-oedema type I, the large majority of cases, has low antigenic and functional C1-INH, whereas type II has a normal or raised antigenic level but reduced function from a dysfunctional protein
Attacks are non-pitting, non-pruritic angio-oedema without urticaria, affecting skin, the gastrointestinal tract (severe colicky abdominal pain that can mimic a surgical abdomen) and the larynx
Laryngeal involvement is the principal cause of death and can progress to asphyxiation, so airway attacks are emergencies
Because attacks are bradykinin-driven rather than histamine-driven, they do not respond to antihistamines, corticosteroids or adrenaline
A persistently low C4 is a useful screening clue, being reduced during and usually between attacks; C1-INH antigenic level and function confirm the diagnosis
Acquired C1-INH deficiency, associated with lymphoproliferative and autoimmune disease, presents in later life and is distinguished by a low C1q

Attacks may be precipitated by trauma, dental or surgical procedures, infection, oestrogens and angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibitors; management separates long-term prophylaxis, procedural prophylaxis and acute treatment
reference.pathophysiology: C1 esterase inhibitor, encoded by SERPING1, is the major plasma inhibitor of several serine proteases: activated C1r and C1s of the classical complement pathway, the mannose-binding lectin-associated serine proteases, and, critically for symptoms, plasma kallikrein and activated factor XII of the contact system, as well as components of the fibrinolytic cascade. Heterozygous loss-of-function variants (type I) or variants producing a dysfunctional protein (type II) reduce effective C1-INH activity below the threshold needed to restrain the contact system. Unopposed activated factor XII and kallikrein activity then liberate bradykinin from high-molecular-weight kininogen; bradykinin acting on endothelial B2 receptors increases vascular permeability, producing the localised, self-limiting subcutaneous and submucosal oedema of an attack. Uninhibited classical pathway activity explains the characteristically low C4. In the acquired form, C1-INH is depleted or neutralised by autoantibodies or by consumption associated with lymphoproliferative disease, giving a similar bradykinin-mediated phenotype but with additional consumption of C1q.
additionalDifferentials: Histaminergic (mast cell-mediated) angio-oedema, with or without urticaria, including allergic and idiopathic angio-oedema
Acquired C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency associated with lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disease
Hereditary angio-oedema with normal C1-INH (for example factor XII, plasminogen or angiopoietin-1 variants)
Other causes of an acute abdomen when gastrointestinal attacks dominate
Anaphylaxis when laryngeal or mucosal swelling is prominent
additionalInvestigations: Serum C4 as an initial screen, which is typically low
C1 esterase inhibitor functional assay to detect type II disease
C1q level to distinguish the acquired form from hereditary deficiency
SERPING1 gene analysis where the diagnosis is uncertain or for family studies
Investigation for underlying lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disease when the acquired form is suspected
redFlags: Laryngeal or tongue swelling with voice change, difficulty swallowing or stridor, indicating impending airway obstruction
Rapidly progressive facial or neck swelling
Severe unexplained recurrent abdominal pain with vomiting suggesting a gastrointestinal attack
First presentation of angio-oedema in later life, prompting a search for the acquired form and an underlying disorder
reference.prognosis: With modern acute treatments and prophylaxis most patients achieve good symptom control and a near-normal life expectancy, although untreated laryngeal attacks can be fatal. The disease is lifelong and attack frequency varies widely between and within individuals.
pitfalls: Treating attacks as allergic and relying on antihistamines, corticosteroids and adrenaline, which are ineffective for bradykinin-mediated angio-oedema
Missing type II disease by measuring only the antigenic C1-INH level and not its function
Overlooking the diagnosis in patients presenting with recurrent unexplained abdominal pain
Failing to distinguish the acquired form (low C1q, later onset, underlying disease) from hereditary deficiency
Prescribing angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibitors or oestrogen-containing preparations, which can precipitate or worsen attacks
references: Allergy and clinical immunology reference texts
management: Treat acute bradykinin-mediated attacks with C1-inhibitor concentrate, the bradykinin B2-receptor antagonist icatibant, or a kallikrein inhibitor such as ecallantide, and do not rely on antihistamines, corticosteroids or adrenaline
Manage laryngeal attacks as airway emergencies with immediate specific therapy and readiness to secure the airway by intubation or surgical means

Provide long-term prophylaxis for frequent or severe attacks with C1-inhibitor replacement, the anti-kallikrein antibody lanadelumab or oral berotralstat, using attenuated androgens or antifibrinolytics where these are unavailable
Give short-term prophylaxis with C1-inhibitor concentrate before dental, surgical or other high-risk procedures
Advise avoidance of triggers, particularly ACE inhibitors and oestrogen-containing contraceptives, and manage infection and trauma as precipitants
Train patients in self-administration, provide an emergency action plan and ensure on-demand therapy is carried at all times
Monitor attack frequency, treatment response and quality of life
Offer genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal dominant SERPING1-related inheritance
